newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Pacific Forum readmits France as dialogue partner.
newsitem.headline: Pacific Forum readmits France as dialogue partner.

text.p: South Pacific Forum members on Thursday readmitted France as a dialogue partner and vowed to lead the charge for the U.N. adoption of a nuclear test ban treaty.
The 16-nation group welcomed the end of French nuclear testing in the South Pacific and said they had agreed to readmit France as a dialogue partner with immediate effect.

"Leaders look forward to the resumption and further development of constructive relationship at a regional level with France," the leaders said in a statement at the end of their three-day meeting in the Marshall Islands.
France was suspended from the forum last year in protest at its final series of nuclear tests in French Polynesia which ended in January this year.

"The suspension imposed after dialogue talks last year has been a significant and effective part of the region's campaign against nuclear testing," the leaders said in the statement, which was received here.

The Pacific Forum decided to lift the suspension in light of France's permanent cessation of testing, its signing of the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty in March and its support for a Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT).
But with post-forum dialogue talks starting on Friday, it is unlikely France will be able to attend at such short notice.
In Paris, a Foreign Ministry spokesman welcomed the action.
"France welcomes the decision by the South Pacific Forum to readmit it as a dialogue partner," spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters at the ministry's daily briefing.

The annual forum brings together leaders from Australia, the Cook Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Nauru, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Western Samoa.
Forum leaders also called for all U.N. members to sign the CTBT.
"By permanently banning nuclear testing, the CTBT would secure invaluable nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament benefits and enhance international security," the forum leaders said.
Australia plans to introduce a resolution at the U.N. General Assembly starting on September 9 calling for the stalled CTBT to be voted on, despite opposition to the treaty from India.
New Delhi, which exploded a nuclear device in 1974 but has denied possessing atomic weapons, says the treaty is flawed.
The forum leaders said they "expected members to take the lead in the United Nations by early co-sponsorship of the CTBT resolution".
"Forum leaders urged all nations to join with them in signing and ratifying the CTBT as soon as possible, to facilitate the treaty's earliest implementation," they said.

But the leaders backed away from a call by Papua New Guinea to extend the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty to ban the shipment of nuclear weapons through the region, referring the plan to a committee for a report.
The Pacific leaders also said the forum "would welcome Malaysia as a post-forum dialogue partner".
With many Pacific states facing economic crisis, the leaders agreed to hold an annual economic ministers summit, the first in Australia in 1997, and for aid to be tied to economic reforms.
